introduce verb

a person to someone

also introduce someone, introduction, letter of introduction, may I introduce, I’d like to introduce you to

classical

Cic. Fam. 7.5.3: tōtum dēnique hominem tibi ita trādō
Hor. Epist. 1.9.3: ut tibi sē laudāre et trādere cōner
Traupman 16–17, 334, 147

trādō, trādere, trādidī, trāditum

verb, third conjugation; with an accusative of the person and a dative · Conjugation on Wiktionary

introduce, recommend (a person to someone)

Properly “hand over”: Cicero and Horace use it in letters introducing a friend to a great man (Cic. Fam. 7.5.3; Hor. Epist. 1.9.3). Traupman’s dialogue has velim trādere tibi cōnsōbrīnam meam, “I’d like to introduce my cousin to you”.

Other words

  • commendō, commendāre, commendāvī, commendātum — recommend, introduce (especially by letter)

    verb, first conjugation; with an accusative and a dative · also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 7.17.2: sīc eī tē commendāvī et trādidī · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    A letter of introduction is litterae commendāticiae (Cic. Fam. 5.5.1, Lewis & Short).

  • dēdūcō, dēdūcere, dēdūxī, dēductum — take (a young man) to a teacher or a patron

    verb, third conjugation; with ad and the accusative · also used · classical · Cic. Amic. 1: ā patre ita eram dēductus ad Scaevolam · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    Lewis & Short: “to conduct a young man to a public teacher”.

Examples

  • tōtum dēnique hominem tibi ita trādō, dē manū, ut ajunt, in manum tuam istam et victōriā et fidē praestantem

    In short, I hand the whole man over to you, from my hand, as they say, into that hand of yours, so outstanding in victory and in good faith.Cic. Fam. 7.5.3

  • Septimius, Claudī, nīmīrum intellegit ūnus, quantī mē faciās, nam cum rogat et prece cōgit scīlicet ut tibi sē laudāre et trādere cōner

    Septimius, Claudius, is plainly the only one who knows how much you think of me: for he asks, and begs me, if you please, to try to commend and introduce him to you.Hor. Epist. 1.9.1–3

  • ego autem ā patre ita eram dēductus ad Scaevolam sūmptā virīlī togā, ut, quoad possem et licēret, ā senis latere numquam discēderem

    When I had put on the toga of manhood, my father took me to Scaevola, and so, as far as I could and was allowed, I never left the old man’s side.Cic. Amic. 1

  • Velim trādere tibi cōnsōbrīnam meam.

    I’d like to introduce you to my cousin.Traupman 16

See also pleased to meet you, know, friend.
